passage:
Layla ran the student food-bank drive in Lyon, answered every friend's 2 a.m. messages, and cried at the end of films she had seen five times. This week she had sorted four hundred tins, stayed up with Olga after a break-up, and argued with her flatmate about the dishes at midnight.
On Thursday she sat on the kitchen floor, too tired to open the fridge.
Olga found her there. 'You carry everyone. Who carries you?'
Layla laughed, then cried. 'I don't know how to care less.'
'Don't care less. Care on a schedule.' They made a list together: dinner at seven, no matter what. Phone off at midnight. The dishes talk would wait till Sunday morning, when she wasn't exhausted.
On Sunday the talk took ten calm minutes.

qa.q: How many tins had Layla sorted this week?
qa.a: Four hundred tins.

qa.q: What does Layla sitting on the kitchen floor, too tired to open the fridge, show?
qa.a: It shows she was overwhelmed and exhausted from giving so much to everyone at once.

qa.q: Which choice about the dishes talk made it go better?
qa.a: Waiting till Sunday morning, when she wasn't exhausted, turned a midnight argument into ten calm minutes.

qa.q: How does Olga see Layla's way of caring?
qa.a: Olga values how much Layla carries but worries that nobody carries her, so Olga suggests caring on a schedule rather than caring less.

grounding: Shows a young adult who gives everything to friends and causes and gets exhausted, then learns routines and better timing for hard talks.

passage:
In the college theatre club's green room, Trisha had been the first to arrive and the last to leave for three weeks. She painted sets, rewrote scenes at 3 a.m., and still took every late call from her roommate, who was going through a rough patch. On the night of the dress rehearsal she forgot her own lines twice and burst into tears in the wings.
Manoj, the final-year student directing the play, sat on an upturned crate beside her. 'Your fire is why this play works,' he said. 'But you can't pour it all out every day and expect any left.'
She wiped her face. 'I don't know how to do half.'
'Not half. Rhythm. Sleep by one. One day off a week. And tell your roommate you'll talk at lunch, not at three in the morning.'
Trisha nodded slowly.

qa.q: When did Trisha rewrite scenes?
qa.a: At 3 a.m.

qa.q: What made Trisha burst into tears in the wings?
qa.a: Exhaustion from giving everything to the play and to her roommate caught up with her, and forgetting her lines twice tipped her over.

qa.q: What choice does Manoj ask Trisha to make, and why?
qa.a: To keep a rhythm: sleep by one, a day off each week, and roommate talks at lunch, so her depth of feeling doesn't drain her completely.

qa.q: How might Trisha's roommate feel about talking at lunch instead of at 3 a.m.?
qa.a: The roommate may feel a little let down at first but may also get a more rested, attentive Trisha.

grounding: Shows a young adult pouring herself into a passion and a roommate's troubles until she is overwhelmed, and learning rhythm and timing to keep going.

passage:
Salma,
I owe you an explanation for last Thursday. You saw me cry in the middle of the campaign meeting, over a poster. The truth is, I've been giving everything to the tree-protection drive: three meetings a week, the petition, the night vigils. I love it. I also haven't slept properly in a month, and when you asked about the date change, it felt like the last straw. That's not on you. I've made some changes. No campaign messages after ten. Sunday mornings are for cricket and my mother's parathas. And when I need to raise something hard, like my frustration with how the committee runs, I'll do it on a rested day, not at midnight. I still care as much. I just want to still be here next year.
Divyansh

qa.q: How many meetings a week has Divyansh been going to?
qa.a: Three meetings a week.

qa.q: What was Divyansh feeling in the campaign meeting?
qa.a: Divyansh felt overwhelmed and exhausted, so a small question felt like the last straw.

qa.q: What changes is Divyansh making to protect the passion?
qa.a: No campaign messages after ten, Sunday mornings kept free, and hard talks saved for rested days.

qa.q: How might Salma feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Salma would likely feel relieved that the tears weren't about Salma, and glad Divyansh is making changes to stay well.

grounding: Shows a young adult who gives everything to a cause, gets overwhelmed, and builds routines and better timing for hard talks.

passage: I'm Harsha, and I do friendship at full volume. When Ritu's father was ill last year, I was at the hospital every evening, cooking, making calls, carrying her bags. I'd do it again. But by the end of that month I was so drained I slept through my own exam. And when Ritu said, gently, that she needed a quiet day, I took it as rejection and cried for hours. It's all big for me: the love, the hurt, the tiredness. What's helping now is pretty boring. I sleep at the same time every night. I walk every morning. And when I need to have a hard talk, I wait till I've eaten and slept, not the minute I'm upset. The waves still come. I'm just learning to surf them.

qa.q: What did Harsha sleep through?
qa.a: Harsha's own exam.

qa.q: How did Harsha feel when Ritu asked for a quiet day?
qa.a: Harsha felt rejected and hurt, crying for hours, because every feeling runs big.

qa.q: What routines are helping Harsha?
qa.a: Sleeping at the same time, walking every morning and waiting to have hard talks until rested and fed.

qa.q: How might Ritu have felt about Harsha's help during her father's illness?
qa.a: Ritu was probably grateful and cared for, though she also needed some quiet time.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult whose intense friendships bring both devotion and exhaustion, and who learns routines to ride the waves.

passage:
Monday: Arohi stayed up till three helping her roommate Sonali through a break-up, then organised the hostel's flood-relief drive before breakfast, buzzing with purpose.
Wednesday: Exhausted, she snapped at the warden, cried in the stairwell and wanted to have it out with Sonali right then about the borrowed clothes. She stopped herself: "Not now. Not tired."
The next Monday: She had slept properly two nights running and kept her morning run. That evening, calm, she raised the clothes with Sonali. It took five minutes. They laughed. The relief drive was still going, and so was she.

qa.q: What did Arohi organise before breakfast on Monday?
qa.a: The hostel's flood-relief drive.

qa.q: How was Arohi feeling on Wednesday?
qa.a: She was exhausted and overwhelmed, snapping and crying in the stairwell.

qa.q: Which choice helped Arohi most, and why?
qa.a: Waiting to talk to Sonali until she was rested, because the hard talk then took five minutes and ended in laughter.

qa.q: How might Sonali experience the talk about the clothes?
qa.a: Sonali likely found it easy and friendly, since Arohi raised it calmly.

grounding: Shows over days a young adult whose passion leads to overwhelm, and who learns timing and routine to keep going.

passage:
You want to fix the whole world by Friday, Gargi. I know that look. I had it at twenty.
In my final year, your Shankar Mama ran the flood relief drive at college. I slept four hours a night, answered every phone call, and cried in the bus when a donor backed out. My roommate Pritam would leave a plate of rice on my desk, and I wouldn't touch it.
Then, in the middle of a meeting, I snapped at the one girl who was helping most. She walked out.
That night Pritam said, "You care like a flood yourself. A flood destroys too." It stung. After that, I kept Sunday mornings for sleep and cricket, and I waited till I was calm before hard talks.
We kept the drive going for two more years. So care deeply, beta. Just eat the rice.

qa.q: Who left a plate of rice on Shankar Mama's desk?
qa.a: His roommate Pritam would leave a plate of rice on his desk.

qa.q: How was young Shankar feeling during the relief drive?
qa.a: He was overwhelmed and exhausted; he slept four hours a night, cried in the bus and snapped at the helper he relied on most.

qa.q: What turning point in the story let Shankar keep caring without collapsing?
qa.a: After Pritam's words, he kept Sunday mornings for rest and waited until he was calm before hard talks, so the drive lasted two more years.

qa.q: How might Pritam have seen his roommate in those weeks?
qa.a: Pritam seems worried and caring; he quietly brought food and later told Shankar the honest thing he needed to hear.

grounding: Shankar Mama tells Gargi how his intense caring at twenty exhausted him until routines and better timing for hard talks let him keep his depth.
